stimulus.text:
Dunmore: “And I do hereby further declare all indentured Servants, Negroes, or others, (appertaining to Rebels,) free that are able and willing to bear Arms, they joining His MAJESTY'S Troops as soon as may be, for the more speedily reducing this Colony to a proper Sense of their Duty, to His MAJESTY'S Crown and Dignity.” — Lord Dunmore's Proclamation, November 7, 1775 (abridged)

Virginia Convention: “We think it proper to declare, that all slaves who have been, or shall be seduced, by his lordship's proclamation, or other arts, to desert their masters' service, and take up arms against the inhabitants of this colony, shall be liable to such punishment as shall hereafter be directed by the General Convention. . . . we hereby promise pardon to them, they surrendering themselves to Col. William Woodford, or any other commander of our troops, and not appearing in arms after the publication hereof.” — Virginia Convention, December 14, 1775 (abridged)
stimulus.source_note: Lord Dunmore's Proclamation, November 7, 1775, and Virginia Convention declaration, December 14, 1775. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus viewed before writing — Lord Dunmore's Proclamation (November 7, 1775) and the Virginia Convention's reply (December 14, 1775), public domain. Different questions from the 3.5 Dunmore set (0510-0512).

books.section: Topic 3.6 The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals, A. The Call for Egalitarianism

stem: The two passages together best support which conclusion about the Revolution's ideals?

options.text: Both sides agreed that slavery must end once the war was over
options.misconception: Neither passage looks past the war, and Virginia's side defends slavery outright; no agreement to end it appears anywhere.

options.text: Dunmore issued his proclamation out of abolitionist conviction
options.misconception: Dunmore's offer is limited to rebels' enslaved people who bear arms; it is a weapon of war, not a moral stand against slavery.

options.text: Enslaved people used wartime promises to seek freedom, while neither side offered emancipation
Virginia's leaders freed the people they themselves held enslaved
options.misconception: Virginia's leaders did the opposite: they threatened death for those who fled and offered only pardon for return to bondage.

rationales.C: Enslaved Virginians weighed two offers — freedom for British service, pardon for return — and hundreds chose the British side. Background: neither side's offer was emancipation; each was a wartime bargain.
rationales.A: No agreement to end slavery appears; Virginia defends the institution while Dunmore exploits it.
rationales.B: Conviction would free all enslaved people; Dunmore frees only rebels' people who fight, which is tactics, not abolition.
rationales.D: Virginia's leaders kept their own enslaved people and threatened those who fled; no freeing appears in the passage.
rationales.general:
1. Ask who acts. Enslaved people, choosing between two offers in wartime.
2. Ask what each offer is. Freedom for service from Dunmore, pardon for return from Virginia.
3. Ask what neither offers. Emancipation as a principle — both bargains serve the war, not the ideal.
Remember: ideals move people even when no side honors them — follow who acts on the words, not who speaks them.
